message.content:
Here’s a quick rundown of some of the most celebrated American composers—both historical and modern—who have left an indelible mark on U.S. music:

| Composer | Era | Notable Works / Contributions |
|----------|-----|--------------------------------|
| **John Philip Sousa** (1854–1932) | Late 19th – early 20th c. | “Stars & Stripes Forever,” “The Washington Post March.” Known as the “March King.” |
| **Scott Joplin** (1868–1917) | Early 20th c. | “Maple Leaf Rag,” “The Entertainer.” Pioneer of ragtime. |
| **George Gershwin** (1898–1937) | 1920s–30s | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris.” Blended classical with jazz/pop. |
| **Aaron Copland** (1900–1990) | Mid‑20th c. | “Appalachian Spring,” “Fanfare for the Common Man.” Iconic “American” sound. |
| **Leonard Bernstein** (1918–1990) | Mid‑20th c. | “West Side Story,” “Candide.” Broadway maestro and conductor. |
| **Philip Glass** (born 1937) | Contemporary | Minimalist works such as “Glassworks,” “Einstein on the Beach.” |
| **John Adams** (born 1947) | Contemporary | Pulitzer‑winning “Nixon in China,” “Short Ride in a Fast Machine.” |
| **Steve Reich** (born 1936) | Contemporary | Minimalist pieces like “Music for 18 Musicians,” “Different Trains.” |
| **William Grant Still** (1895–1978) | Mid‑20th c. | “Afro-American Symphony.” First African‑American symphony composer. |
| **Charles Ives** (1874–1954) | Early‑mid 20th c. | Experimental “Concord Sonata,” “The Unanswered Question.” |

These figures span from the birth of American popular forms (ragtime, jazz‑classical hybrids) to the avant‑garde of minimalism and beyond. Their influence continues to shape both concert halls and popular culture across the country.
